He stressed the importance of close cooperation between Bangladesh and The Gambia, particularly during Bangladesh’s FM’s Presidency of the UN General Assembly, to keep the Rohingya crisis high on the global agenda and advance efforts towards a comprehensive and sustainable solution, including the safe, dignified and voluntary return of the Rohingyas to Myanmar.

item.title: Five-year-old child killed in Rohingya camp gunfight
item.description:
A five-year-old child was killed in a gunfight between armed groups at the Kutupalong Rohingya camp in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, on Thursday evening.
The child, identified as Mojahed, sustained a gunshot wound to the head during the firing. His mother Tahera Begum and 6 others were also injured.
The gunfight took place around the B-40 and B-41 blocks of Camp-8 East at Kutupalong.
Police initially suspect that the gunfight took place between members of the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) and the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO).
Police Superintendent Asaduzzaman, deputy commander of the 8-Armed Police Battalion (APBn) assigned to Ukhiya, disclosed the incident on Friday morning.
Police and local sources said gunfire suddenly began in the camp on Thursday evening. More than 100 gunshots were heard, prompting many people to leave their homes and seek shelter.
Mojahed, son of Nur Alam, a resident of Camp-8 East, was rescued in critical condition and taken to Cox’s Bazar District Sadar Hospital. He died while undergoing treatment.
Among the seven injured, three were women, including Mojahed’s mother. Some of the injured were transferred from Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital to Chittagong Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
A drive is underway to identify and arrest those involved in the incident.

item.title: Saudi fire victim returns home after eight years, buried in Rajshahi
item.description:
Shyamal Uddin Majhi, who was killed in a fire at a sofa manufacturing factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was buried beside his parents at his family graveyard in Bagmara, Rajshahi, at 11am on Friday.
His body reached his home in Dangapara village of Marugram under Jhikra Union of Bagmara upazila at around 3am on Friday.
The bodies of Shyamal and 9 other Bangladeshis arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at around 4pm on Thursday. The bodies were then handed over to the relatives of the deceased.
Shyamal was a resident of Marugram under Jhikra Union of Bagmara upazila in Rajshahi district. His son-in-law Mizanur Rahman went to the airport to receive his body.
Mizanur said Shyamal’s namaz-e-janaza was held at 11am on Friday, with relatives and local residents attending. He was later buried beside his parents at the family graveyard.
Shyamal had gone to Saudi Arabia around 8 years ago in the hope of improving his family’s financial condition. He worked at a sofa manufacturing factory in the Manfuhah area of Riyadh.
On the night of August 9, a fire broke out at the factory, killing 16 Bangladeshi workers, including Shyamal.
Family members had been waiting for Shyamal to return home after 8 years. According to family sources, he had been preparing to return and had told them during their last conversation that he would return home soon.
His wife and 3 daughters had been waiting for him. His death has left the family facing uncertainty, as he was the family’s only earning member.
Local residents have called on the government, elected representatives, affluent individuals and those involved in expatriate welfare to stand beside the bereaved family.
Bagmara Upazila Nirbahi Officer Selim Ahmed said: “After hearing about the death, the upazila administration provided Tk 25,000 and dry food. They also received Tk 35,000 at the airport. Since the deceased has 3 daughters, I have asked prominent people in the area to look after them. As they are studying, we will support them.”

item.title: Ismail Ould elected new OIC secretary general
item.description:
Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed has been elected secretary general of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
The Mauritanian diplomat and former foreign minister took the oath of office, succeeding Hissein Brahim Taha, in the presence of foreign ministers from OIC member states.
Earlier, OIC member states elected him as the new secretary general of the Islamic body during the 23rd Extraordinary Session of the Council of Foreign Ministers, held at the OIC headquarters in Jeddah on Thursday.
In his address, the newly elected secretary general said his election was the greatest honour of his career and the highest distinction he had received after more than three decades of international, regional and national service.
He added that his pride in receiving the trust was unparalleled, as was his determination to live up to the expectations of the organization’s member states and prove through actions, not just words, that his selection as secretary general was justified.
For her part, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates of the State of Palestine Dr Varsen Aghabekian Shahin thanked the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for inviting the meeting and for its steadfast support of the Palestinian cause.
She pointed to attacks by Israel, the occupying power, on countries in the region and said Israel had become emboldened to act against them because it had enjoyed impunity for decades.
The minister called on member states to take practical, political and legal measures to hold accountable those responsible for settler crimes and those who support and finance them.
She stressed that incursions, violations and attempts to alter the historical and legal status quo in Al-Quds (Jerusalem) and the Al-Aqsa Mosque constitute a direct threat to peace and stability in the region.

item.title: Nepal-Tibet border buried in death, devastation
item.description:
Rescue teams waded through mud on Thursday searching for more than 1,400 people missing after flash floods and landslides struck the Nepal-Tibet border, as the death toll rose sharply to at least 362, with entire villages swept away.
Experts warned of the risk of further floods a day after the devastating tsunami-like wall of freezing water and mud wiped out towns under a torrent of sludge, engulfing homes, smashing bridges and dams, and sweeping vehicles away like toys.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.
Emergency teams were racing to pluck survivors from affected zones, while Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under the suffocating dirt.
“Everything is finished,” Omkar Joshi, a 35-year-old Nepali customs agent rescued from a hilltop in the border town of Timure, told AFP.
“It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood.”
Nepali police said they had recovered 359 bodies.
Another 910 people, including 517 foreign tourists, were out of contact in the country. Beijing said 100 Chinese citizens are missing in Nepal.
In China, state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, are missing.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the area on Thursday, state media said, to oversee “emergency rescue and relief work, and to visit rescue workers and affected people”.
Li Qipu, a member of China’s paramilitary People’s Armed Police, cited “the instability of a reservoir lake upstream” and “the narrow mountain road” as elements complicating rescue efforts.
China’s Tibet Autonomous Region is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists.
‘Inland tsunami’
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the Himalayan nation to “stand together” hours after the disaster, visited some of the hardest-hit areas on Thursday.
Shah told local authorities to “provide immediate relief to displaced families” and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.
The foreigners out of contact included Indians and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, Nepal’s tourism board said.
The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami”, travelling nearly 170 kilometres south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia’s La Trobe University.
Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected, but deaths were reported as far south as Chitwan, on the border with India.
Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, who lives in exile in India, said he would “pray for all those who have lost their lives”.
Chinese government officials in Tibet mobilised nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, the official Xinhua news agency said.
Promises of aid and assistance came in soon after reports of the scale of the disaster.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was sending emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.

item.title: Bangladesh urges OIC states to fund Gambia’s Rohingya ICJ case
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Thursday called upon the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) member states to contribute to the voluntary trust fund established to support The Gambia’s case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concerning the atrocities committed against Rohingyas by Myanmar.
He also urged them to strengthen international efforts for the safe, dignified and voluntary repatriation of the Rohingyas to Myanmar.
The state minister made the call while speaking at the 23rd OIC Extraordinary Council of Foreign Ministers (CFM) in Jeddah.
In his statement, Kobir welcomed the newly elected Secretary General of the OIC, Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, and assured him of Bangladesh’s full support and cooperation throughout his tenure.
He underscored the OIC’s important role as the second-largest intergovernmental organisation in advancing the interests and wellbeing of the Muslim Ummah.
The state minister expressed appreciation for the contributions of the outgoing secretary general and hoped that the new secretary general will build upon the positive institutional developments achieved during the previous tenure.
Reiterating Bangladesh’s unequivocal support for the Palestinian cause, he reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to a just and lasting solution based on the two-state solution, with an independent and sovereign State of Palestine living alongside Israel in peace and security.
Kobir expressed gratitude to the OIC member states for their support for the election of Bangladesh’s foreign minister as president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (PGA).

item.title: How an avalanche unleashed Nepal catastrophe
item.description:
A massive ice-and-rock avalanche in Nepal’s high Himalayas appears to have temporarily dammed a river before the blockage collapsed, unleashing the catastrophic flood that tore through the Nepal-China border region on Wednesday, scientists say, as authorities warn the danger of further flooding has not passed.
The disaster sent a wall of water, mud and boulders down the Bhotekoshi river corridor, devastating settlements and infrastructure and leaving a heavy death toll and hundreds unaccounted for.
According to the Kathmandu Post, scientists analysing satellite imagery increasingly believe an avalanche blocked the Lhende river, creating a temporary natural dam. When that barrier gave way, the accumulated water surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi.
Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, a climate researcher and professor at Kathmandu University, told the newspaper that an avalanche on the Nepal side was suspected of blocking the Lhende.
A magnitude-4.4 earthquake was recorded in Tibet around the same time, but scientists have yet to establish whether it contributed to triggering the avalanche.
The Kathmandu Post also cited journalist Kunda Dixit of Nepali Times as reporting that an avalanche struck the northern face of the 7,245-metre Langtang Lirung, sending debris into the river system.
Scientists at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) are examining satellite imagery to establish the precise sequence of events.
Preliminary evidence indicates a huge volume of ice and rock entered the Lhende, possibly accumulating at a narrow section and forming a temporary landslide dam, according to the Kathmandu Post.
The scale of the resulting surge was extraordinary.
The newspaper, citing ICIMOD, reported that the Trishuli river rose by as much as nine metres within 30 minutes at Galchhi and about seven metres at Malekhu.
The region was already considered highly vulnerable.
A sudden Bhotekoshi flood in July last year was attributed to a glacial lake outburst near the Nepal-China border.
Research by ICIMOD and the UN Development Programme has identified 3,624 glacial lakes across Nepal, India and Tibet, 47 of them potentially dangerous.
The latest disaster has also renewed concerns over the increasing instability of the Himalayan cryosphere as temperatures rise.
“The risk is still there,” Kayastha told the Kathmandu Post, warning that warming increases the likelihood of glacier melt, ice-and-rock collapse and avalanches, although scientists cannot predict exactly where the next disaster will strike.
That warning has taken on added urgency with the formation of another large barrier lake.
This report was compiled from reporting by the Kathmandu Post and Global Times, with the latter citing Chinese government agencies and state media.

item.title: Bangladeshi among 15 killed in fire at Russia’s Amur gas complex
item.description:
A Bangladeshi worker was among 15 people killed in a fire at the Amur Gas Chemical Complex (AGCC) in Russia’s eastern Amur region on Tuesday, the Bangladesh Embassy in Moscow said Thursday.
Another Bangladeshi worker remains missing, while seven others were seriously injured, said Mizanur Rahman, the embassy’s first secretary (labour).
The deceased was identified as Zakir Hossain, from Bhairab in Kishoreganj. The missing worker, Md Alal Hossain Raju, is from Gangni in Meherpur.
Mizanur said some bodies were badly burned and could not yet be identified. Raju may be among the unidentified remains, he said.
According to Reuters, AGCC initially reported seven deaths, including six Chinese nationals, on Wednesday. The company later raised the death toll to 15 in a post on its Telegram channel on Thursday, saying 14 of the dead were foreign nationals.
AGCC said the fire originated in an auxiliary section of a pyrolysis unit before spreading. The complex’s main equipments were not damaged, it said. Mizanur said arrangements were underway to transfer the seven seriously injured Bangladeshi workers from Amur to a specialised hospital in Moscow. Six are currently in intensive care.
The embassy has contacted the relevant authorities to arrange the repatriation of Zakir’s body. The embassy will also continue discussions with LLC Sinopec Engineering Group regarding Zakir’s outstanding dues and compensation, Mizanur said.
The embassy has already prepared the required attestation and other documents for repatriating the body.

item.title: Barrier lake threatens fresh deluge in flood-hit Nepal
item.description:
A massive barrier lake formed in northern Nepal following Wednesday’s devastating floods and mudslides is already overflowing and faces a high risk of breaching within the next three days, raising fears of another destructive surge as rescuers search for hundreds of missing people.
China’s Ministry of Water Resources estimated the lake contained around 2 million cubic metres of water as of Thursday morning, while another 3 million cubic metres could flow into it over the next three days, according to China Central Television, as reported by the Global Times.
The development threatens to compound a disaster that has already devastated communities along the Nepal-China border and left hundreds missing, including large numbers of foreign nationals.
According to the Kathmandu Post, the barrier lake has formed near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers in Nepal.
Chinese authorities said the lake was already overflowing and warned that continued inflows could trigger a breach.
Chinese Ministry of Water Resources is monitoring its development and conducting flood simulations to assess how a sudden release of water could affect downstream areas and emergency operations.
The Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo originate in Tibet and merge before crossing into Nepal, where the river is known as the Bhotekoshi, a major upper tributary of the Trishuli.
A breach could unleash another sudden surge downstream, posing fresh risks to communities and infrastructure along a river system already battered by Wednesday’s disaster.
The warning comes as Nepal and China continue massive rescue operations following the catastrophic floods and mudslides along their border.
The disaster struck Nepal’s Rasuwa region on Wednesday morning before causing severe destruction around the border.
Roads, bridges, buildings and other infrastructure were swept away or damaged as floodwaters and debris surged through the area and downstream.
The Global Times reported Thursday that rescue operations were being complicated by continued rainfall, unstable terrain and the danger of secondary disasters, including the newly formed barrier lake.
Chinese authorities have mobilised emergency responders, military personnel, engineering teams and aircraft for rescue and relief operations.
Authorities on both sides of the border are still working to establish the full scale of the casualties and locate those missing.
Chinese officials said hydrological monitoring and simulations would continue as authorities prepare for the possibility of the barrier lake giving way.

item.title: Dhaka offers help as Nepal reels from deadly floods
item.description:
Bangladesh has offered assistance to Nepal as devastating flash floods and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 362 people and left several hundred missing, prompting Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman to express solidarity with the disaster-hit country.
Prime Minister Tarique expressed deep shock over the loss of lives and conveyed condolences on behalf of the government and people of Bangladesh to Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah and the people of Nepal.
“We stand ready to extend any support that Nepal may need at this time of distress,” Tarique said in a condolence message.
The disaster struck the Nepal-Tibet border region on Wednesday, with flash floods and landslides devastating settlements and leaving a trail of destruction.
Aid workers said entire settlements had been “wiped out”, while footage from the affected border region showed a massive surge of debris sweeping away vehicles and infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Khalilur on Thursday followed up Bangladesh’s offer of assistance in a phone conversation with his Nepalese counterpart Shisir Khanal.
Terming the disaster a “terrible tragedy”, Khalilur conveyed Bangladesh’s condolences and said the country stood ready to provide whatever assistance Nepal might require.
He said no casualty involving a Bangladeshi national had been reported so far and sought the Nepalese government’s cooperation should any Bangladeshi be found among those affected.
Khalilur also conveyed Tarique’s personal condolence message to the Nepalese prime minister and reaffirmed Dhaka’s solidarity with Kathmandu.
The Nepalese foreign minister thanked Bangladesh for its support and said authorities were still assessing the full extent of the devastation.
Nepal would communicate any specific assistance it required from Bangladesh once the comprehensive damage assessment was completed, he said.
The diplomatic outreach comes as rescue teams continue searching for hundreds of people whose whereabouts remain unknown following one of the region’s deadliest recent flood disasters.
Bangladesh’s offer leaves the nature and scale of possible assistance open until Nepal identifies its requirements, with Dhaka signalling its readiness to respond once Kathmandu completes its assessment.

Third Terminal inches closer to take-off after years of delay
item.description:
The long wait to bring Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s Third Terminal into operation could finally end in December, with aviation authorities completing the evaluation of a Japanese company’s proposal to run the facility and preparing to enter the crucial negotiation stage.
The Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) has completed its assessment of the company’s technical and financial proposals, clearing a major hurdle towards an operating agreement for the terminal, which has remained largely unused despite being virtually complete for years.
Negotiations are expected to begin in the first week of September, with officials aiming to sign a final agreement in October and proceed with a limited-scale soft opening on December 16, according to CAAB sources.
The development provides the clearest timeline yet for making the Tk-thousands-of-crores aviation infrastructure operational after prolonged uncertainty over who would operate and maintain it.
The Japanese company submitted its Request for Proposal (RFP) to CAAB last Tuesday. An evaluation committee subsequently assessed its technical capability before reviewing the financial proposal.
S M Lablu Rahman, CAAB member (Administration) and chairman of the proposal evaluation committee, said the evaluation process had been completed.
“As the next step, we will hold discussions with the Japanese company. After the discussions, there will be an agreement. We are moving toward our target of a soft opening by December 16,” he told Bangla Tribune.
“We hope we will be able to complete everything within the stipulated time.”
Construction of the Third Terminal began on December 30, 2019, and it was ceremonially soft-opened in October 2023 after more than 99% of the project was completed.
Yet passengers have not been able to use the facility for regular operations for nearly three years amid delays in finalising its operation and maintenance arrangements.
Air Commodore Abu Sayeed Mehboob Khan, CAAB member for Operations and Planning and vice-chairman of the evaluation committee, said the RFP followed lengthy discussions with the Japanese side.
“If everything goes well, we hope we will be able to reach a final agreement within a short time,” he said.
“If everything remains in order, it will be possible to open the terminal on December 16 as announced by the government.”
Preparations are meanwhile underway for the proposed opening, including system testing, recruitment and staff training, security arrangements and coordination among immigration, airlines, ground handlers and other agencies.
The 230,000-square-metre terminal is expected to dramatically expand the country’s main international airport.
The existing first and second terminals can handle around 8 million passengers annually; with the Third Terminal operational, total capacity is expected to rise to as many as 20 million passengers a year.
It will have parking facilities for 37 aircraft, 100 check-in counters, 10 self-check-in kiosks, 16 regular baggage belts and four dedicated belts for oversized baggage.
The terminal also includes automated baggage-handling facilities, modern baggage storage, airline lounges, baby-care facilities, children’s play areas, health inspection and first-aid rooms, disease-testing facilities and an isolation area.
For CAAB, however, the immediate challenge is no longer construction but turning the completed infrastructure into a functioning airport terminal.
If negotiations begin as scheduled in September and culminate in an agreement in October, December 16 could finally mark the beginning of passenger operations at a terminal that has spent years waiting for take-off.

item.title: David Emon’s second-in-command Mobarak held after Fatikchhari shootout
item.description:
Police arrested notorious criminal Mobarak Hossain from the false ceiling of a washroom in Fatikchhari, Chittagong, following a tense hours-long operation on early Wednesday.
Mobarak is known as the second-in-command of jailed top criminal David Emon and is allegedly involved in several killings, including the murder of Jubo Dal leader Masud in Raozan.
He opened fire at police from the false ceiling during the raid, firing six rounds and injuring five police personnel, including Chittagong Additional Superintendent of Police Kazi Md Tarek Aziz.
Police arrested him after his firearm jammed. Three of his associates, Md Raihan, Md Farid and Md Nasir, were also arrested from the house.
Acting on a tip-off, police surrounded a house in Shahnagar area of Lelang Union around 3am on Tuesday. After the occupants refused to open the iron gate, police broke it down at around 4:30am in the presence of local residents.
Officers entered the house and found Mobarak hiding in the washroom’s false ceiling. He opened fire as police approached, injuring five officers.
The injured include Additional SP Tarek Aziz, Fatikchhari Police Station OC Robiul Alam Khan, Aziz’s bodyguard Constable Mamunur Rashid, and Constables Shah Newaz and Saddam Hossain. They received medical treatment.
Tarek Aziz, who led the operation, said police had learned of Mobarak’s whereabouts after arresting David Emon on July 29. Several raids were subsequently conducted in the remote hills of Fatikchhari, but Mobarak evaded arrest.
On Monday, police arrested four of his associates, Arafat, Md Munna, Iqbal and Babul, during a raid in the Kanchannagar hills.
Police said Mobarak later left the hills and took shelter at a house belonging to an acquaintance in Shahnagar, apparently considering it safer.
Tarek Aziz said police found Mobarak’s associate Raihan hiding inside the false ceiling above a washroom after entering the house. He was arrested from there. Police later detained two other associates, Nasir and Farid, from inside the false ceiling.
“Since the criminals could open fire on police from inside, the operation team proceeded cautiously. At one point, Mobarak was found hiding in the false ceiling of a washroom inside one of the rooms. As police entered the room, he opened fire with a Brazilian-made Taurus pistol. Police returned fire.
“Mobarak fired six rounds, while police fired seven. One of the bullets passed close to Tarek Aziz’s ear. Mobarak’s pistol jammed when he attempted to fire the seventh round. Police then brought him down from the false ceiling and recovered the weapon.
“The pistol had been looted from Kotwali Police Station in Chittagong city on August 5, 2024. After Mobarak’s arrest, police conducted raids in Fatikchhari and Raozan until 10pm on Wednesday to recover more weapons.”
Tarek Aziz said police sought Mobarak’s remand in two cases—one over the looting of the firearm and another over the attack on police. On Thursday, a court granted him eight days’ remand—four days in each case.
The remand was granted in the two separate cases filed with Fatikchhari Police Station over the weapon theft and attack on police.
Superintendent of Chittagong Police Md Masud Alam said Mobarak was a notorious criminal who used remote hilly areas as safe hideouts, making it difficult for police to arrest him.
“Acting on a tip-off, police arrested Mobarak and his associates. He has admitted to involvement in several killings, including the murder of Jubo Dal leader Masud in Raozan,” he said.
Police recovered a 9mm foreign-made pistol, a 7.65mm foreign-made pistol, a foreign-made revolver and a locally made pistol, along with ammunition, three magazines and spent bullet casings.

item.title: Lotus blooms turn Kalijug Beel into natural kaleidoscope
item.description:
White lotus flowers have transformed Kalijug Beel in Pirganj into a picturesque natural attraction, drawing thousands of visitors from different parts of the country.
The wetland, located in Kalijug village of Jabarhat Union, about 13 kilometres south of Pirganj upazila town of Thakurgaon, is now covered with blooming lotuses.
The sight is particularly striking in the early morning and late afternoon, when the white flowers sway gently in the breeze against the tranquil backdrop of the wetland.
Visitors start arriving early in the morning, with families, friends and groups gathering to enjoy the scenery and take photographs. A wooden footbridge is currently the only access route into the lotus-covered area.
Local residents said the naturally formed lotus wetland has become one of the area's most popular attractions. They, however, urged visitors to protect the environment and refrain from damaging or plucking the flowers.
Shahana Parvin, who came from Dinajpur while visiting relatives in Ranisankail, said she decided to visit the site after hearing about it.
“Having boats to take visitors around the beel would make the experience even better,” she said.
School student Nigar said she had heard about Kalijug Beel only a few days earlier and persuaded her parents to take her there.
“I was happy to see so many lotus flowers, but I felt bad when I saw some people plucking them,” she said.
Nafisa, who visited the beel with two friends from Bangladesh University of Professionals in Dhaka, said they were fascinated to see a lotus wetland after reading about such places in books and magazines.
She suggested developing the area in a planned manner by introducing boating facilities, restaurants, washrooms and better transport links.
“With proper planning and basic facilities, this place could attract many more tourists,” she said.
Chan Bania, a resident of Kalijug village, said visitors arrive at the beel every day from distant areas.
“Our homes are located just west of the beel. Many visitors enter our houses without permission, which makes us uncomfortable,” he said.
Pirganj Upazila Agriculture Officer Agriculturist Nazmul Hasan said lotus is an aquatic plant that spreads naturally.
“Lotus seeds can be carried by birds and fall into wetlands, from where new plants grow and gradually spread,” he said.
He added that Kalijug Porabeel is now extensively covered with lotus flowers and has emerged as a tourist attraction.
Professor Abu Bakkar Siddique, former principal of Thakurgaon Government Women's College, said lotus flowers have several medicinal properties.
He said the flower was once common in Bangladesh's wetlands but has become increasingly rare as many wetlands and water bodies have been filled or degraded.
“Steps should be taken to expand lotus growth and conserve the flower considering its importance,” he said.
Pirganj Upazila Nirbahi Officer Golam Rabbani Sardar said the naturally grown white lotuses had added a unique dimension to the area's natural beauty.
“It is truly pleasing to see people coming here from different places,” he said.
He urged visitors to enjoy the beauty without damaging the environment or plucking the flowers.
The local administration, in coordination with the union parishad, will maintain necessary monitoring to protect the area and preserve the wetland, he added.

item.title: River dredging project stalled as Sunamganj haor farmers face triple crisis
item.description:
A long-delayed river dredging project has left hundreds of thousands of Boro farmers in Sunamganj facing a triple crisis of flash floods, waterlogging and irrigation shortages.
Farmers say the failure to restore the drainage capacity of the region's rivers is delaying rice transplantation, creating irrigation problems during the dry season and increasing the risk of crop losses from early monsoon rains.
Sunamganj is one of the country's major Boro-producing districts. About 350,000 farmers cultivate Boro rice on around 223,000 hectares of land every year. In a normal season, the district produces approximately 1.15 million tonnes of paddy, equivalent to about 950,000 tonnes of rice.
Despite decades of investment in flood-protection embankments, the lack of regular river dredging has severely disrupted the natural drainage system of the haor region. Farmers say embankments alone cannot protect their crops if rivers and canals cannot drain water efficiently.
The district has witnessed devastating flash floods in 1990, 1994, 2004, 2010, 2016, 2017 and 2022, when breaches in crop-protection embankments allowed upstream water to inundate vast areas of farmland. The losses ran into thousands of crores of taka, affecting hundreds of thousands of farmers.
The crisis has become more complex in recent years. In 2024, water levels in the haors and adjoining rivers remained almost the same, resulting in severe waterlogging that submerged immature Boro rice on around 80,000 hectares of farmland.
Farmers say the problem now occurs in two stages. During the dry season, sediment-filled riverbeds hold little water, creating an acute irrigation shortage. During the pre-monsoon period, the same rivers fail to drain water quickly, causing waterlogging that can destroy standing crops.
Sofor Uddin, 66, a farmer from Astama village in Joykalas Union of Shantiganj upazila, said farmers are increasingly trapped between late transplantation and early flooding.
“Water does not drain from the haor into the rivers on time, so transplantation starts about 15 days late. By then, irrigation water becomes scarce. Then even a little rain at the beginning of Baishakh can submerge the immature crop,” he said.
Abdur Rahman, a farmer from Dariyabaz village in Mollapara Union of Sunamganj Sadar upazila, said he cultivated six bighas of land with borrowed money last season, only to lose the entire crop to waterlogging after rainfall at the beginning of Baishakh.
“For a farmer, the loss of one crop can create a debt that takes years to repay,” he said.
According to Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), Sunamganj has 106 rivers and river channels across its 12 upazilas. Although most carry substantial volumes of water during the monsoon, around 70 become largely dry during the dry season.
The district's location near the Meghalaya hills of India further increases its vulnerability. Heavy rainfall in the upstream hills sends large volumes of water downstream within a short period, triggering flash floods. At the same time, sediment carried by the runoff gradually raises riverbeds, reducing their capacity to carry and drain water.
Bijon Sen Roy, former general secretary of Haor Bachao Andolon, said eight transboundary rivers—including the Chilai, Khasiyamara, Jadukata, Chela, Sonali Chela and Maula—along with more than 100 hill streams carry large volumes of water from Meghalaya into Sunamganj during the monsoon.
He said water from much of Sylhet also flows through the Surma and Kushiyara rivers before reaching the Meghna through the Dhanu River. Years of inadequate dredging have severely disrupted this interconnected drainage system.
“During the monsoon, the rivers are overflowing, but in the dry season many of them become almost completely dry. This indicates that the natural water-management system has been seriously damaged,” he said.
Retired professor Chittaranjan Talukdar, a former president of the Communist Party of Bangladesh's Sunamganj district unit, said river dredging has repeatedly been promised after major floods but has not been implemented on the required scale.
Md Obaidul Haque Milon, general secretary of the Sunamganj Haor and River Protection Movement, also called for immediate implementation of the dredging project.
“Authorities talk about river dredging whenever there is a disaster, but years pass without the project reaching the implementation stage,” he said.
The BWDB has proposed a major dredging project to address the problem.
BWDB Sunamganj Executive Engineer Mamun Hawlader said the proposal, titled ‘Improvement of Early Flood Management and Integrated Water Resources Management in the Haor Region,’ has been sent to the Ministry of Water Resources for approval.
The proposed Tk 1,429.84 crore project includes dredging 304 kilometres of 13 rivers, including the Surma, Kushiyara, Baulai, Dhanu, Ghura-utra, Upper Meghna, Old Surma, Chamti Darain, Abua, Patlai, Kaunai and Someshwari.
The proposed implementation period is 2026–2029, but the project has yet to receive approval.
“If approved, the project will improve water drainage, reduce waterlogging and help address irrigation shortages in the haor region,” Hawlader said.
Prabir Kumar Goswami, supervising engineer of the Water Development Board's North-Eastern Regional Office, said Sunamganj's location at the foot of the Meghalaya hills makes it naturally vulnerable to flash floods and water-management problems.
He said huge quantities of sediment are carried downstream every year by water flowing from the Indian hills, gradually raising the beds of rivers, canals and haors.
“Years of inadequate river dredging have made the problem increasingly severe,” he said.
With the next Boro season approaching, farmers fear that the unresolved dredging issue will once again expose them to the same cycle of delayed transplantation, irrigation shortages and waterlogging. They are urging the government to approve and implement the proposed project before another season of crop losses begins.

item.title: Three snakes found on 19th floor of secretariat
item.description:
Three snakes were found in the corridor of the Education Ministry on the 19th floor of Building No 6 at Bangladesh Secretariat on Thursday, raising questions about how they reached such a high floor.
Officials and employees first spotted two snakes in the corridor after arriving at work in the morning. Another snake was seen in the same area a short while later.
The offices of the education minister and education secretary are located on the same floor.
Officials who witnessed the incident said the snakes were seen moving through the corridor, causing panic among ministry officials and employees.
Ministry employees later killed all three snakes.
However, their species could not be immediately identified.
The ministry’s public relations officials confirmed the incident on Thursday afternoon and expressed surprise at finding three snakes together on the 19th floor of the Secretariat.
They said there could be more snakes inside a storeroom or elsewhere in the building, adding to concerns among officials and employees.
The incident has also raised questions about how the snakes managed to reach the 19th floor and whether there are other snakes inside the building.

item.title: Speaker: Disorder could threaten parliament’s functioning
item.description:
Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad Bir Bikram has warned that continued shouting, discourteous behavior and violations of parliamentary rules could seriously threaten Parliament’s functioning.
He made the remarks during the third session of the 13th National Parliament on Thursday following a commotion and exchange of words over statements by Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed and the opposition leader.
“The Rules of Procedure must be strictly followed to keep the democracy achieved through many sacrifices functioning and to make this institution of the people effective,” he said.
“The opposition has full freedom to point out the shortcomings and lapses of the government. But shouting in unison and silencing a minister without allowing him to finish his statement cannot be a healthy parliamentary practice.”
Recalling his nearly 40 years of parliamentary experience, the speaker referred to the bitter history of the past and urged lawmakers to learn from it and work toward building a better Parliament.
The opposition leader later resumed the discussion, referring to past instances in which statements were removed from parliamentary proceedings or sent for review.
He said the home minister’s remarks were clearly unparliamentary and alleged that similar incidents had occurred repeatedly.
He also questioned the speaker’s impartiality and protested the Speaker’s remarks that the treasury bench had more members.
The opposition leader said he did not support dividing Parliament based on numbers or status. He said the opposition would support the government on good initiatives and protest against wrongdoing.
He expressed hope that the speaker would conduct proceedings impartially and ensure equal dignity for all lawmakers.
Lawmaker Md Manirul Haque Chowdhury raised a point of order after part of his budget speech was removed from the proceedings for telling a metaphorical story.
He asked the speaker which word in his statement had been deemed unparliamentary.
Manirul also alleged that remarks about his beard and religious beliefs had undermined his personal dignity and the dignity of Parliament.
Seeking protection of his dignity, he asked the Speaker to respond formally to the notice and sought a resolution and ruling on the matter.
Responding to the overall situation, Hafiz Uddin said he had not been present when the incident involving Manirul occurred and would review the proceedings.
He said necessary action would be taken if anything unparliamentary was found.
“It is extremely regrettable that members are being prevented from speaking in the way they are,” he said.
The Speaker warned that Parliament could not function for long if lawmakers failed to follow his direction to sit down when asked.
Expressing disappointment over the disorder, he urged all sides to exercise patience.
The session was later adjourned for Asr prayers.

item.title: 30 ministers, state ministers, whips assigned to oversee law and order among other things in 64 districts
item.description:
The government has assigned 30 ministers, state ministers and whips of Parliament to oversee and coordinate overall government activities in all 64 districts, including maintaining law and order, combating corruption and drug abuse, and ensuring good governance, transparency and accountability.
The information was disclosed in a gazette notification signed by Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani on Thursday.
The assignments will take immediate effect.
According to the notification, the government has expressed concern that development allocations in various districts had previously been misappropriated through widespread corruption, with part of the proceeds allegedly siphoned abroad and the rest used for activities involving drugs, social degradation and threats to public and state security.
Against this backdrop, the ministers, state ministers and whips have been given the responsibility of supervising and coordinating district-level activities related to law and order, corruption and drug control, good governance, transparency and accountability, as well as development and public welfare programs.
Under the distribution of responsibilities, Iqbal Hassan Mahmood has been assigned Rajshahi and Natore, while Dr Abu Zafar Md Zahid Hossain will oversee Lalmonirhat, Nilphamari and Panchagarh. Abdul Awal Mintoo has been given responsibility for Lakshmipur.
Nitai Roy Chowdhury will oversee Chuadanga, Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, Habiganj; and Ariful Haque Choudhury, Moulvibazar.
Md Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee has been assigned Chittagong. M Rashiduzzaman Millat will oversee Sherpur, Mymensingh and Netrokona, while Asadul Habib Dulu will oversee Thakurgaon and Dinajpur.
Md Asaduzzaman has been assigned Khulna, Satkhira and Bagerhat, while Zakaria Taher will oversee Feni and Noakhali.
Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain will oversee Manikganj and Munshiganj, while Sa Ching Prue has been assigned Cox's Bazar.
Md Shariful Alam will oversee Tangail and Narsingdi; Shama Obaed Islam Madaripur and Shariatpur; and Aninda Islam Amit Meherpur, Kushtia and Jhenaidah.
Abdul Bari has been assigned Bogra and Chapainawabganj; Sultan Salauddin Tuku Dhaka; and Mir Mohammed Helal Uddi Khagrachhari, Bandarban and Rangamati. Habibur Rashid will oversee Gazipur and Narayanganj.
Md Razib Ahsan has been assigned Barguna, Patuakhali and Pirojpur; Mir Shahe Alam Rangpur, Gaibandha and Kurigram; and Farzana Sharmin Sirajganj and Pabna.
Shaikh Faridul Islam will oversee Jessore, Magura and Narail, while Yasser Khan Choudhury has been assigned Jamalpur and Kishoreganj.
Ahammad Sohel Monzoor will oversee Barishal, Bhola and Jhalakathi, Md Shamim Kaiser Joypurhat and Naogaon; and GK Gaus Sylhet and Sunamganj.
Mia Nuruddin Ahmed has been assigned Rajbari, Faridpur and Gopalganj, while ABM Ashraf Uddin will oversee Brahmanbaria, Comilla and Chandpur.
The notification said the assigned ministers, state ministers and whips will advise government offices on controlling drug abuse and illegal trafficking, preventing smuggling and curbing serious crimes to maintain and improve the overall law and order situation in their respective districts.
They will also supervise and provide guidance on implementation of the government's election manifesto, poverty alleviation, employment generation, social safety-net programmes and various development and public welfare initiatives.
If necessary, they may attend district-level meetings and provide advice on relevant issues, according to the notification.
It further said the assignments were made in accordance with the existing powers of the prime minister and the government and decisions of the Cabinet, without undermining the legal authority of local government institutions or other constitutional and statutory bodies.

item.title: Kader Gani Chowdhury appointed BSS MD, chief editor
item.description:
The government has appointed senior journalist Muhammad Kader Gani Chowdhury as managing director and chief editor of the state-run news agency Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS).
The Ministry of Public Administration issued a gazette notification in this regard on Thursday.
According to the notification, Kader Gani Chowdhury has been appointed under the Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha Act, 2018, on a contractual basis for one year.
His appointment will take effect from the date of his joining and is subject to his relinquishing any employment or professional engagement with any other profession, business, or government, semi-government, or private institution or organization.
Kader Gani Chowdhury replaces Md Kamal Uddin Mozumder, better known as Kamal Uddin Shabuj, who was appointed BSS managing director and chief editor on April 7.
Kader Gani Chowdhury has long been involved in journalism. He is currently serving as secretary general of the Bangladesh Federal Union of Journalists (BFUJ), the apex platform of journalists in Bangladesh.

item.title: ACC sues ex-land minister, 28 others over Tk141C Aramit Cement scam
item.description:
The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has filed three cases against former land minister Saifuzzaman Chowdhury and 28 others over the alleged embezzlement and laundering of Tk 141 crore through Aramit Cement.
The cases accuse the defendants of withdrawing funds from Islami Bank’s Jubilee Road branch in Chittagong using fake bills and vouchers for the purported purchase of cement raw materials, despite no actual transactions. The funds were allegedly transferred and converted through various bank accounts before being laundered to the UAE, UK, US and other countries.
ACC Deputy Director and Public Relations Officer Aktarul Islam disclosed the information on Thursday.
The accused include Saifuzzaman Chowdhury, his wife and Aramit Cement Managing Director Rukhmila Zaman, former UCB PLC chairperson; Aramit Cement CFO Mohammad Shah Alam; Imperial Trading proprietor Md Abdul Aziz; and officials of various banks and related institutions.
Of the 29 accused, 27 were named in the first case, 16 in the second and 20 in the third.
According to the case documents, Saifuzzaman allegedly used his influence as Aramit Group owner and then land minister to secure loan approvals, falsely portray an Aramit employee as the owner of a supplier, and facilitate the transfer, conversion and cash withdrawal of the funds before laundering them abroad.
He was also accused of purchasing assets in the UAE, UK, US and other countries with the laundered money and identified as the ultimate beneficiary and mastermind of the alleged scheme.
Rukhmila Zaman was accused of facilitating the transactions as UCB chairperson and Aramit Group managing director, using her influence to secure loan approvals and assisting in the transfer and laundering of the funds.
Aramit Cement CFO Mohammad Shah Alam and Imperial Trading proprietor Md Abdul Aziz were also accused of facilitating fake applications and deal approvals, as well as the transfer, conversion and cash withdrawal of the funds.
According to the ACC, the first incident took place on March 20, 2018. A case filed by ACC Assistant Director Sajib Ahmed accuses 16 people of embezzling Tk 57.60 crore through a deal in the name of Imperial Trading, a customer of First Security Islami Bank’s Agrabad branch, based on an application submitted by Aramit Cement’s Jubilee Road branch.
The second incident occurred between April 4, 2018 and December 26, 2019. According to the case documents, Tk 41.625 crore was allegedly embezzled through 17 deals in the name of Imperial Trading, a customer of United Commercial Bank’s Kamal Bazar branch, following an application by Aramit Cement, a customer of Islami Bank’s Jubilee Road branch. ACC Deputy Director Md Mashiur Rahman filed the case against 27 people.
The third incident took place between August 6, 2020 and March 28, 2021. According to the ACC, nine deals were made in the name of Imperial Trading, a customer of United Commercial Bank’s Sadarghat branch, based on applications from Aramit Cement. The case alleges that Tk 42.075 crore was embezzled after excluding the customer’s equity of Tk 4.675 crore. ACC official Shoaib Ibn Alam filed the case against 20 people.

item.title: Could Syria become the focus of an Israeli-Turkish conflict?
item.description:
Following US mediation, Syrian and Israeli representatives met in Jordan last weekend for the first time in months. The talks aimed to defuse tensions following the recent Israeli attacks on Syrian territory and prevent hostilities between Israel and Turkiye from spilling over into Syria.
The escalation was sparked by an Israeli attack on the Abu Duhur military airfield in Syria’s Idlib Province on August 18. According to Syrian sources, the attack struck the runway and storage facilities without causing any fatalities. Israel stated that Syria had violated — or threatened to violate — a previous security agreement by allowing Turkish troops to use the airfield. The governments of both Syria and Turkiye rejected these allegations.
The United States criticized the attack by its Israeli ally as an “unnecessary escalation.” In diplomatic terms, this amounts to a fairly clear show of rhetorical support for Ankara and Damascus.
Israel views a potential Turkish military presence in Syria as a red line. Yet, it remains unclear whether such a deployment is planned in the long term or whether it was even imminent at the time of the attack. Evidence on this matter is not publicly available.
However, as early as April 2025, Reuters news agency cited anonymous sources saying Turkiye had inspected at least three air bases in Syria where it might want to station troops as part of a planned joint defense pact. Israeli airstrikes were already taking place at that time as well.
The Washington-based think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), which is considered pro-Israel, justifies the attack as follows: “Israel worries that Ankara could eventually use its military presence in Syria as a platform to pressure or threaten Israel, and remains wary of the close relationship between Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa and the Turkish leadership.”
For Bente Scheller, Syria expert at the German Green Party-affiliated Heinrich Böll Foundation, this explanation falls short.
“There is no evidence so far that Turkish troops are actually supposed to be stationed there,” she told DW. While Israel may indeed have its own intelligence, the recent attack must be viewed against the backdrop of Israel’s overall policy toward Syria as well as Turkiye’s growing regional role, she noted.
Marcus Schneider, a Middle East analyst at Germany’s Friedrich Ebert Foundation — which is affiliated with the German Social Democratic Party (SPD) — in Beirut, also points out that a struggle for power and influence is unfolding in Syria and beyond.
“The attack primarily raises the question of what kind of military order will emerge in Syria in the future,” he told DW. In his view, Israel wants to keep Syria weak, as a sovereign state that controls its own airspace would restrict Israel’s military freedom of action. “The corridor for attacks against Iran runs through Syria,” explained Schneider. A sovereign Syria could therefore pose a strategic obstacle to Israel.
Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, Israel’s heightened security concerns are understandable, adds Scheller. In addition, Israel is certainly viewing with concern another development that extends beyond Syria.
“Israel is undoubtedly aware of how Turkiye is currently attempting to position itself as a regional hegemon,” Scheller said. The attack on Abu al-Duhur is therefore “clearly also a message to Turkiye.”
Turkiye supports Syrian President al-Sharaa and is committed to a unified Syria which includes the territory in the country’s northeast, where the majority of Syria’s Kurdish population is located. For years, Turkiye has been attacking the former Kurdish-led autonomous zone along its southern border. On Tuesday, the commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces announced the official dissolution of the group.
An analysis by the US think tank Carnegie Foundation describes the situation as a strategic rivalry between Israel and Turkiye: “The northeast is also the main arena where two externally driven strategic visions for Syria collide.” The International Crisis Group also views Syria as a fault line between Turkiye, a rising regional power, and Israel.
Syria’s improved relations with the US — which amount to US support — offer new prospects for the country, despite the Islamist past of its new leader, President Ahmad al-Sharaa. In summer 2025, the US began gradually easing sanctions, and in November of that year, al-Sharaa was received by US President Trump at the White House. The two met again on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara in July 2026. In early 2026, the US withdrew its military forces from Syria, and on Monday (August 24), it officially removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
However, under the current circumstances, Syria appears to be relying primarily on itself, including in its relations with Turkiye. For analyst Marcus Schneider, however, a potential Turkish presence is not comparable to the former Iranian presence during the Assad regime.
Contrary to the view held in Israel, he argues that Ankara is primarily interested in a stable Syria and in securing its southern border. “The idea that Turkiye, a Nato member, would attack Israel, a nuclear power, is preposterous,” he said. The real problem, he argues, is that Israel increasingly views Turkiye as a strategic adversary and interprets Turkiye’s capabilities as evidence of hostile intentions.
Al-Sharaa is seeking foreign policy support wherever he can find it, observes Scheller. “In recent months, Turkiye has increasingly become one of the countries from which Damascus expects concrete assistance.” This is not just a matter of security: Ankara wants to expand its regional influence and, at the same time, has an interest in maintaining stability along the shared border, she said.
Following the overthrow of Syria’s longtime ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, Israel established a security zone north of the Golan Heights and has repeatedly attacked Syrian targets. According to an analysis by the Carnegie Foundation, the calls for such a buffer zone is deeply rooted in Israeli security thinking; less clear, however, is the intention — sometimes attributed to Israel by analysts — of permanently fragmenting Syria to keep it weak.
The US think tank FDD takes a different view, pointing to Israel’s skepticism toward the new Syrian military and Turkish support. However, Schneider notes that the new regime in Syria has extended a hand to Israel from the outset, despite its ideological origins. “Damascus does not want a war with Israel,” he said, adding that it wants to regain its national sovereignty. It is precisely this aspiration that clashes with Israel’s military presence and its red lines.
“Syria is caught between two militarily powerful neighbors that respect neither its sovereignty nor its territorial integrity,” said Scheller.
In her view, the outcome will now depend on al-Sharaa’s negotiating skills. “How can he defend Syrian sovereignty against these two neighbors and actually chart a distinct Syrian path?” However, Syria’s weakness does not lie solely in its military inferiority. The country must first develop a viable political order, she notes.
This is also the starting point for political scientist Haid Haid in an analysis for the British think tank Chatham House: “Syria’s foreign policy success has been significant, but it cannot, on its own, secure stability. In this sense, Syria’s greatest vulnerability lies not at its borders, but within.”

item.title: Death toll from Algeria wildfires rises to 12
item.description:
Forest fires killed 12 people and injured dozens in northeastern Algeria on Wednesday, the interior minister and civil protection authorities said.
The tolls rose from earlier local media reports of two deaths and an unspecified number of injuries in coastal Bejaia province, around 300 kilometers (190 miles) from the capital Algiers.
Five people were killed in Jijel province, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou province, Interior Minister Said Sayoud told national television.
A further 54 people were being treated for burns, including six serious cases, at a hospital in Bejaia, he said.
An eight-year-old boy and a 22-year-old woman were among those killed in Bejaia, a local radio station reported.
Sayoud and Health Minister Mohamed Seddik Ait Messaoudene had travelled to Bejaia to “assess the progress of firefighting operations on the ground... and the condition of the injured,” the official APS news agency reported.
Many residents in Bejaia and Jijel have been evacuated, according to the civil protection agency and local media.
As of 8pm (1900 GMT) on Wednesday, firefighters were battling 69 blazes, the civil protection agency said.
Images broadcast by local site Jijel News showed panicked residents taking refuge in a post office as thick clouds of smoke billowed around them.
Three major national highways connecting regions in the east of the country were closed due to forest fires near the cities of Bejaia, Jijel and Setif, the gendarmerie said.
The civil protection agency said it had deployed significant resources to combat the blazes, which are being fueled by strong winds.
Forest fires occur regularly in northern Algeria during the summer, but climate change is amplifying their impact by causing increasingly frequent droughts and intense heat.
More than 30 people were killed in July 2023 when fires tore through thousands of hectares of forests and farmland, as well as hundreds of homes, in the area around Bejaia.
Authorities recorded nearly 2,000 fires nationwide in July this year.
More than 100 people had to temporarily flee their homes in Annaba in late July as fires swept through the northeastern province, damaging nearly 150 homes.
Official investigations often end with arrests for suspected arson. Four people in Constantine province have been placed in pre-trial detention in connection with the July fires.

item.title: Germany reports record 15,800 heat-related deaths this summer
item.description:
Germany has registered a record 15,800 heat-related deaths this summer as Europe struggles through a series of punishing heatwaves, the national public health institute said Thursday.
The worst affected group were people over 75, and around 9,600 deaths were recorded in one week in late June when Germany baked in temperatures over 40°C, said the Robert Koch Institute (RKI).
Another 4,000 heat-related deaths were recorded between late July and mid-August, said the institute in its latest update.
Heat and drought have battered much of Europe this summer, fueling a spike in heat-related mortality, wildfires, devastating many crops and dropping water levels in major rivers. France, Britain and Spain have all reported thousands of excess summer deaths.
The institute said it has collected heat mortality data for the past decade and that the previous record was 8,900 deaths in 2018. A separate report by a medical publication had estimated 10,000 heat deaths in 1994.
Extreme heat can kill through heatstroke but mostly proves fatal when combined with existing conditions such as cardiovascular, lung or kidney diseases.
The RKI models heat-related mortality using statistical methods that compare deaths during summer weeks with and without heatwaves.
Climate change and heat adaptation were on the agenda of a two-day cabinet retreat this week led by conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz, but no new measures were announced.
Merz said Germany’s 16 states are primarily responsible for heat protection and are already set to receive 100 billion euros ($116 billion) over the next 12 years from a special infrastructure and climate protection fund.
“There is no shortage of programs or of funds,” Merz said Wednesday, adding that the government would examine potential aid for the agricultural and forestry sectors after drought and forest fires.
The parliamentary chief of Merz’s CDU party, Thorsten Frei, meanwhile rejected a proposal by center-left SPD ministers to anchor climate protection in the German constitution as a joint task of national, state and local governments.
This model would carry the risk “that one level of government points the finger at another, and ultimately little gets done,” he told Deutschlandfunk radio.
The group Environmental Action Germany charged the government was “irresponsible” because it had “failed to adopt a single effective measure for heat protection following an extreme summer that saw thousands of heat-related deaths.”
It urged legal changes and funding to help municipalities and cities unseal paved surfaces that store heat and to plant vastly more trees.
“Future summers will be even hotter,” said the group’s director Barbara Metz. “Yet instead of finally ensuring our cities remain livable and people stay healthy, the government is merely tinkering with the symptoms.”

Measles outbreak: Death toll 955 as five children die in 24 hours
item.description:
Five more children died with measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours until 8:00am on Thursday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 955 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all five latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With these, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 856, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 99, it said.
A total of 956 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to153,692.
Meanwhile, 75 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 18,726.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 134,437 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 129,489 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

item.title: Salahuddin: Improvement in law and order now visible, suspects being arrested in 24-48 hours
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Thursday told Parliament that an improvement in the country’s law-and-order situation is now visible, with law enforcement agencies arresting alleged perpetrators and bringing them to justice within a short time after crimes are committed.
“The improvement in the law-and-order situation is visible in Bangladesh. Since the present government took charge, whenever a crime has occurred, the perpetrators have been arrested and brought under the law within 24 to 48 hours or even less time,” he said.
The minister made the remarks, while replying to a supplementary question from National Citizen Party (NCP) lawmaker Md Abul Hasnat (Comilla-4) in the House.
Responding to the lawmaker’s concerns over the law-and-order situation, he said police and other law enforcement agencies have made prompt arrests in several cases, including those that drew significant public attention.
“From the Ramisa case to the four recent murders in Rangpur, the police and other law enforcement agencies have been able to arrest the suspects within the shortest possible time and bring them under the law,” Salahuddin said.
He rejected broad allegations of failure by the Ministry of Home Affairs or law enforcement agencies, saying such claims should be backed by specific incidents and verifiable information.
“If you can point to any specific incident where the ministry or the law enforcement agencies have failed, we can give a detailed response to that particular incident,” the minister said.
He also questioned the basis of crime statistics cited by the lawmaker, saying figures presented in Parliament should be accompanied by their sources and methodology.
Salahuddin recalled that the government previously placed detailed crime statistics before Parliament, including through statements under Rule 300, covering different categories of criminal activities.
Responding to another supplementary question about the number of firearms and the recovery of weapons looted from different places, he said a committee comprising representatives of all relevant forces have been formed to recover the weapons.
The minister said law enforcement agencies are regularly recovering looted firearms and matching their serial numbers to identify them.
“We are continuously recovering weapons, including some of the looted firearms. We match their numbers and inform the media when such weapons are recovered,” he said.
Salahuddin expressed hope that all looted weapons, including those taken from prisons and other locations, will eventually be recovered.
Regarding allegations of political or partisan considerations in police recruitment during the previous government, he said an investigation into the matter is nearing completion.
The minister said investigators have found irregularities involving the recruitment of thousands of police constables and personnel of other ranks in several districts.
In some cases, he said, applicants allegedly changed their addresses to become eligible for recruitment in particular districts, including by purchasing small plots of land and using those addresses as their permanent or village addresses.
Salahuddin said several districts, including Faridpur, Gopalganj, Madaripur, Shariatpur and Kishoreganj, have been identified where such irregularities were allegedly committed.
“We have reached an advanced stage in the investigation. Once it is finalised, we will make the findings public before the nation,” he said.

item.title: Army to build modern arms factory at closed Jalil Textile Mills site in Ctittagong
item.description:
The Bangladesh Army will establish a modern factory on the premises of the closed Jalil Textile Mills at Fouzdarhat in Sitakunda upazila of Chittagong district for producing military equipment and arms, said Chief of Army Staff General Waker-Uz-Zaman on Thursday.
The government formally handed over 54.99 acres of land under the Bangladesh Textiles Mills Corporation to the Bangladesh Army at a symbolic price on Thursday afternoon for the Bangladesh Ordnance Factory (BOF) following an agreement, he said.
The contract was signed between the government and the Bangladesh Ordnance Factories (BOF) of the Bangladesh Army on mill premises as part of the land transfer process.
The factory will help meet the country's demand for arms and could generate substantial foreign exchange by exporting weapons produced there, the Army chief added.
He thanked Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and all concerned for facilitating the land transfer.
“This is not only about meeting the country's needs; the facility will also be developed as an export-oriented industry,” General Waker said, adding that there is demand for Bangladeshi arms in many countries.
If bureaucratic complexities can be removed, Bangladesh could earn significant foreign currency through arms exports, he said.
Explaining the choice of the hilly site at Fouzdarhat, the Army chief said its proximity to Chittagong Port will facilitate the production of modern and sophisticated military equipment and help enhance the country's defence capabilities.
He described the project as part of efforts to strengthen the country's strategic security, saying a long-closed industrial facility will now begin a new chapter in a different form.
Textiles and Jute Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir attended the program as the chief guest.
He said the global defence industry and technology have undergone revolutionary changes, with drones and other military equipment now available at comparatively lower costs in high demand.
The government will provide all necessary support for arms and defence exports, the minister said, adding that the initiative will take Bangladesh to a new level.
Prime Minister’s Defence Adviser Brig Gen (retd) AKM Shamsul Islam and Quartermaster General of the Army Lieutenant General Mohammad Shaheenul Haque were also present.
After the signing ceremony, the minister and the Army chief inspected the abandoned factory premises and later planted trees there.
Jalil Textile Mills began operations in 1961 on around 55 acres of land as a prominent manufacturer of yarn and fabrics. The mill played an important role in the country's textile industry for decades but eventually suffered successive losses and mounting difficulties.
Its production operations were finally shut down in 2004. The premises remained abandoned for years before the necessary procedures and formalities were completed to transfer the land to the Army.
The transfer marks the beginning of a new chapter at a site long associated with the history and heritage of Bangladesh's textile industry.

item.title: Five universities to strengthen systems against campus sexual harassment
item.description:
Five public and private universities will strengthen their institutional mechanisms for preventing and responding to sexual harassment and gender-based violence on campus under a new partnership between the University Grants Commission (UGC) of Bangladesh and UN Women.
The initiative will focus on strengthening internal complaint committees, improving reporting and referral systems, and raising awareness among students and staff about mechanisms for addressing sexual and gender-based violence.
The five universities are Begum Rokeya University, Rangpur; Shahjalal University of Science and Technology (SUST), Sylhet; Khulna University; Daffodil International University; and American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB).
UGC and UN Women formalized the partnership by signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) at the UGC Auditorium in Dhaka on Thursday under UN Women’s European Union-funded Ending Sexual and Gender-Based Violence in Public Spaces, Workplaces and in Tertiary Educational Settings in Bangladesh (ESGBV) project.
The initiative comes amid growing concerns over gender-based violence affecting young women, including technology-facilitated violence.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ (BBS) 2024 National Violence Against Women Prevalence Survey, 16% of women aged 20 to 24 experienced technology-facilitated gender-based violence in the previous year.
Through the ESGBV project, UN Women and its civil society partner Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) will work with the five universities to strengthen their internal complaint committees and institutional mechanisms, improve reporting and referral systems, and raise awareness among students and staff.
The partnership will also support implementation of the 2009 High Court directives on preventing sexual harassment, which require educational institutions and workplaces to establish effective mechanisms to prevent and address such incidents.
The project will also introduce social and behavioral change campaigns at the universities aimed at challenging harmful gender norms and promoting safer and more respectful learning and working environments.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, UGC Chairperson Professor Dr Mamun Ahmed stressed the importance of collective action to ensure that higher education institutions provide safe and enabling environments for students and staff.
“True academic excellence can never be achieved in an environment where fear, harassment and discrimination exist. Our universities must remain spaces where students, especially women, can pursue their dreams, explore their potential and express their intellect without the looming shadow of gender-based violence,” he said.
Representing the European Union, Baiba Zarina, deputy head of delegation and head of the Political, Economic, Trade, Press and Information Section, said the agreement could help turn existing standards into practical measures and strengthen institutional responses.
“Today’s signing matters because it could help translate standards into practice, strengthen institutions and give students and staff the confidence that their concerns will be heard and addressed. The lessons generated here can improve higher education across the whole of Bangladesh,” she said.
UN Women Representative Gitanjali Singh highlighted the importance of strong institutional systems, accountability and coordinated action to prevent violence against women and girls.
“Safe campuses are essential for young women and girls to pursue their education and aspirations. It is our collective responsibility to create safer learning and working environments so women can achieve their full potential without the fear of harassment and violence,” she said.
A discussion moderated by Shrabana Datta, manager of the Ending Violence Against Women Unit at UN Women, also highlighted commitments from the vice-chancellors of the participating universities.
The signing ceremony brought together UGC officials, members of the UGC Executive Committee, vice-chancellors and representatives of the five participating universities, along with representatives of the European Union, UN Women and other stakeholders.
The agreement marks another step in the implementation of the ESGBV project, which seeks to strengthen institutional responses, improve access to complaint and referral mechanisms, increase awareness and address social and institutional attitudes that contribute to sexual and gender-based violence.
The broader goal is to create safer and more inclusive campuses where students and staff can learn, work and participate fully in university life without fear of sexual harassment or gender-based violence.

item.title: Rickshaw council warns proposed rules could create vehicle syndicates
item.description:
The Rickshaw, Battery Rickshaw-Van and Easy Bike Sangram Parishad on Thursday urged the government to reconsider proposed licensing rules for battery-run vehicles, warning they could allow business syndicates to control production, charging and operations.
The demand was made at a press conference in front of the National Press Club in Dhaka.
Reading out a written statement, council Convener Khalequzzaman Lipon said the policy proposed by the Ministry of Local Government on August 17 contains both positive and concerning provisions.
Under the proposal, local government bodies, including city corporations, municipalities, upazilas and union parishads, would issue registration and licenses for electric rickshaws instead of the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA).
The council, however, objected to a provision requiring batteries to be charged only with solar power. It warned that violations could result in license cancellation, non-renewal and fines.
It also opposed any requirement to purchase e-rickshaws from designated manufacturers, saying this could create a powerful business syndicate controlling vehicle production, charging, licensing and operations.
The council said nearly 6 million people depend on the battery-run rickshaw sector for their livelihoods, while millions of commuters rely on the vehicles amid a shortage of affordable public transport.
The leaders called for a unified national policy under the BRTA covering registration, route permits, driver training, licenses and fitness certification, instead of a fragmented licensing system.
They also demanded withdrawal of the solar-only charging requirement, an end to extortion and illegal fees, and permission for all qualified local manufacturers to produce battery-run vehicles without preferential treatment for any particular group.
The council announced plans to submit memorandums to the Road Transport and Bridges Ministry and the Local Government Ministry in the first week of September.
It will also hold divisional and district-level rallies and submit memorandums on September 10.

item.title: PM Tarique mourns deaths in Nepal flash floods
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has expressed deep shock and sorrow over the tragic loss of lives caused by devastating flash floods in Nepal and conveyed condolences to the Nepalese government and people.
In a condolence message on Wednesday, he conveyed heartfelt sympathy on behalf of the government and people of Bangladesh to Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah and the people of Nepal.
"Deeply shocked and saddened to learn of the tragic loss of lives, caused by the devastating floods that have struck Nepal. On behalf of my people and Government, I convey our deepest condolences to Prime Minister Balendra Shah and the people of Nepal," the Prime Minister said.
"Our thoughts and prayers are with those who have lost their lives, and with their families and loved ones as they bear this immense loss. We stand ready to extend any support that Nepal may need at this time of distress," added the prime minister.
A massive flood and landslide disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 160 people on Wednesday and left several hundred missing, many of them foreign tourists.
Aid workers said entire settlements had been “wiped out.” Surveillance footage verified by AFP shows dozens of people running for their lives as a stories-tall surge of debris slammed into the Chinese side of a border area, tossing lorries and buses aside.
